input.instructions: Create a compact, accurate blueprint for an 8-to-12-minute educational lesson with exactly ten sequential teaching beats. Do not write full narration. Create exactly three measurable learning objectives. For every beat, provide one distinct complete factual claim, a concrete example, a concise editable visual direction, and one or two exact supplied source IDs. End the claim, example, and visual direction with complete punctuation. Every cited source excerpt must directly support the claim; reuse at least two important technical terms from each cited excerpt so support can be checked locally. Do not invent course assignments, policies, measurements, datasets, instruction encodings, or product behavior that is absent from the supplied excerpts. Keep the claim, example, and visual direction compact; a deterministic local expander will produce the full narration. Sequence the beats from foundations through application and end with a practical analysis checklist. Use only the supplied source excerpts for factual claims. Every factual claim must cite one or more supplied source IDs. Narration must describe information that is essential to understand visuals. Do not imitate a named creator or invent sources.
input.prompt:
Topic: CSCI-251: Concepts of Parallel and Distributed Systems. Create a representative course-foundations companion aligned to the official catalog description. It must teach durable concepts and problem-solving methods without claiming to replace the instructor's syllabus. Official catalog description: This course is an introduction to the organization and programming of systems comprising multiple computers. Topics include the organization of multi-core computers, parallel computer clusters, computing grids, client-server systems, and peer-to-peer systems; computer networks and network protocols; network security; multi-threaded programming; and network programming. Programming projects will be required. Prerequisites: CSCI-243 or SWEN-262 or equivalent courses. Contact Hours: Lecture 3 Typically Offered: Fall, Spring Regeneration revision 2: use ten distinct, specific beat titles and avoid repeating any title or section label.

Source excerpts:

[mpi-standard]
MPI defines communication among processes identified by ranks in communicators. Point-to-point operations send and receive typed messages between selected ranks. Collective operations coordinate communication patterns such as broadcast, reduction, gather, scatter, and barrier across a group. Blocking and nonblocking operations expose different completion and overlap behavior. Message matching depends on communicator, source, and tag. Distributed-memory programs must partition data and work, communicate required dependencies, and avoid deadlock. Performance analysis considers communication volume, latency, load balance, synchronization, process placement, and the ratio of useful work to coordination overhead.

[openmp-specification]
OpenMP defines a shared-memory parallel programming model based on directives, library routines, and environment variables. A parallel region creates a team of threads. Worksharing constructs divide loop iterations or sections among the team. Data-sharing attributes determine whether variables are shared, private, firstprivate, or reduced across threads. Barriers and other synchronization constructs establish ordering where independent execution is not sufficient. Incorrectly synchronized accesses can create data races. Scheduling choices influence load balance, locality, and overhead. Parallel analysis distinguishes available concurrency, task granularity, dependencies, synchronization cost, memory behavior, and measured scalability.

[rit-csci-251]
This course is an introduction to the organization and programming of systems comprising multiple computers. Topics include the organization of multi-core computers, parallel computer clusters, computing grids, client-server systems, and peer-to-peer systems; computer networks and network protocols; network security; multi-threaded programming; and network programming. Programming projects will be required. Prerequisites: CSCI-243 or SWEN-262 or equivalent courses. Contact Hours: Lecture 3 Typically Offered: Fall, Spring
